en: The Sutra on King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha to Make Offerings, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At the Jeta Grove, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

Honored and revered by all, they came to make offerings: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; the great king, the crown prince, the ministers, and down to the common people—all came to make offerings, providing robes, bedding, food and drink, couches and mats, and medicines for the sick and infirm.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s fame and virtue were heard afar; such was the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. For the sake of sentient beings, he preached the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning was profound and far-reaching, and it was complete with all pure practices.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha addressed his ministers:
"Prepare the state carriages with their feathered canopies. Why is this?

I wish to go to the kingdom of Kāśi-Kosala to pay my respects, prostrate, and serve the World-Honored One. It is extremely rare for a World-Honored One to appear in the world; it is likewise extremely difficult to encounter him. A Tathāgata appears in the world only once in a great while, just as the udumbara flower appears only at certain times; the World-Honored One is just the same—it is exceedingly difficult to meet him."
He replied, "It is so,

Great King! At that time, having heard the command of King Bimbisāra of Magadha— whose countenance was as upright and handsome as a *sāla* tree— the ministers immediately prepared their feather-canopied chariots and went to where King Bimbisāra was, addressing him thus:
"The carriage is prepared; now is the very time.

At that moment, King Bimbisāra of Magadha mounted his feather-canopied chariot, surrounded by his ministers and the populace before and behind him, and departed from Rājagṛha. By the majesty of the king’s power, he proceeded gradually toward Kāśi-Kosala and arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Riding in his carriage as far as the city gate, he alighted from the vehicle and proceeded on foot toward the Jetavana, arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was. Just as a Kṣatriya king discards the five insignia of royal majesty, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, rubbed the World-Honored One’s feet with his hands, and announced his own name:
"I am King Bimbisāra, the king among kings of the kingdom of Magadha; I am King Bimbisāra."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra:

"You are a great king of the noble Kṣatriya clan, while I am a son of the Śākyas who has left the household life to study the Way. Although this physical body of mine is fully endowed with manifold virtues, I have humbled myself by inviting the Great King to my presence to inquire after your health and well-being, and to serve you with palms joined."
The King addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"By the grace of the World-Honored One, I have also seen Kṣatriyas who possess wisdom and great learning, Brahmins who possess wisdom, householders who possess wisdom, and śramaṇas who possess wisdom, each engaging in discussion on the meaning of the Dharma."
"We shall take this treatise and go to question the śramaṇa Gautama. If that śramaṇa Gautama answers with this same treatise, we shall answer him with this treatise;
if the śramaṇa Gautama does not answer with this treatise, we shall likewise engage him in debate. Having said this, they went to where the World-Honored One was.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught him the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One, he no longer asked further questions regarding the meaning of the teachings, much less did he raise any objections.

He then took refuge in the World-Honored One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. This is called the World-Honored One possessing bodily merit, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma, and acting with knowledge of the proper time.

At that time, they attained the three kinds of equal joy; toward the World-Honored One, they further maintained reverence. The great assembly of śrāvakas were pure in all their conduct, accomplished in morality, accomplished in samādhi, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the vision and knowledge of liberation—namely, the four pairs and eight classes of noble ones.

This is called the Blessed One’s assembly of śrāvakas, who are worthy of veneration and honor as the foremost and most venerable; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the people of the world. This is called the third joy in the presence of the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having heard the subtle and wondrous Dharma from the Buddha, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I pray that the Tathāgata will accept my invitation for three months to visit the city of Rājagṛha; I shall provide robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick to the Bhikṣu Saṃgha."
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted King Bimbisāra’s invitation.

Seeing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted his request, King Bimbisāra of Magadha was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew. At the gate of the Jeta Grove, he mounted a carriage adorned with feathered streamers and returned to his own palace in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha commanded his ministers and the people: "Listen well!

I wish to invite the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus for these three months to provide them with offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick. You all should exhort one another to do so."
He replied, "It is so,
Great King! At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, while sitting in a solitary place, had this thought:

"I possess wealth and resources with which I am able to provide for my needs; I wish to provide the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus with robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for illness throughout the remainder of my life, and I shall lead and exhort the ministers and the people to do likewise."
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha immediately exhorted his ministers, saying:
"Just now, while sitting in solitude, this thought arose in me: 'I possess wealth and means to accomplish my purpose;

I wish to provide for the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick—for as long as I live. I ought to command my officials and the people.'"
"O you! Invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus according to your respective capacities; thus, you shall receive inexhaustible rewards throughout the long night.
They replied:
“Thus it is, Great King!
Having heard these instructions from the king, the ministers and the people departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī; he then set out on a journey through the human realm, accompanied by a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, gradually proceeding toward Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that the Buddha had arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, King Bimbisāra commanded his ministers to quickly prepare the state carriage adorned with peacock feathers and proceed to Kalandaka to pay his respects to the World-Honored One.
At that time, having heard King Bimbisāra’s command from the kingdom of Magadha, the ministers went forth to prepare the ceremonial carriage with its feathered canopy.
They reported to Bimbisāra, saying, "The carriage is prepared; now is the very hour."

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha mounted his carriage adorned with feathered streamers, surrounded by his ministers and the populace. Accompanied by the royal majesty, he departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded to the Bamboo Grove at Kalandaka. There, he alighted from his carriage and entered on foot to approach the World-Honored One.

Just as a Kṣatriya king possesses five insignia of majesty—namely, a sword, golden sandals, a parasol, a celestial crown, and a fly-whisk with a jeweled handle—he set them all aside at one side, prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, and sat down to one side.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Since my return to the kingdom, while sitting in solitude, this thought has arisen in me:

'I preside over all the wealth and resources of this realm and am capable of providing for them; I wish to provide for the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus throughout the remainder of my life—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick—and I shall also exhort and lead my ministers and the people so that they may receive deliverance, enabling them to leave the three miserable realms behind for all eternity and dwell forever in peace and security.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra of Magadha:
"Excellent, excellent,
Great King!"

"For the sake of sentient beings, he has conceived the great vow, desiring to bring peace and security to all beings; its principles are profound and far-reaching, so that gods and humans may attain peace.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for King Bimbisāra of Magadha, exhorting and delighting him as he listened, causing all to rejoice.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having heard the subtle and wondrous Dharma from the Buddha, gave rise to a heart of joy. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew. Exiting through the Kalandaka Gate, he returned to his own chariot and proceeded to the city of Rājagṛha. Entering his palace, he sat upon his throne.

On that very day, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink; on that same day, he spread out many seats for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. Holding a censer in his hand, he ascended to the upper story of the high tower and, facing east with palms joined, called upon the World-Honored One with a sincere heart, reflecting to himself: "The time has now arrived; may the World-Honored One, knowing the time, deign to look upon me."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the hour had come, put on his robes and took up his bowl; surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, he entered the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to the palace of King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Having arrived, the community of bhikṣus each sat down in their respective order.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, seeing that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were already seated, took various kinds of sweet and savory foods with his own hands and served them to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. Seeing that the World-Honored One had finished eating and had set aside his bowl, the king spread out a small seat and sat before the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of King Bimbisāra of Magadha, expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma and engaged in gradual discourse with him.

The topics of discussion were the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; he taught that sensual desires are defiled, turbid, and full of outflows, constituting great suffering, whereas renouncing the household life is the essential path.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the king’s heart was filled with such joy he could not contain it and had become entirely gentle and pliant, taught the Dharma as is appropriate for all Tathāgatas—the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and at that moment, the World-Honored One fully expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the king.

At that time, two hundred and fifty maidens attained the purity of the Dharma-eye while still on their seats. Having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, they discerned all phenomena and upheld them; their doubts and hesitations were severed, and their longing was ended. Having attained fearlessness and the dharmas to be studied, they took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and received the five precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw that King Bimbisāra, having heard the subtle and wondrous Dharma, received and upheld it with joy.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Sacrificial fire is the foremost; Verse hymns are also the foremost."
The king is the foremost among men; the ocean is the foremost among all streams.
The moon is the foremost among the stars; the sun is the foremost among luminaries.
Throughout the zenith, the nadir, and the four quarters, he is the sovereign of all created things.
"In the heavens and throughout the world, the Buddha is supreme and without peer;
those who wish to plant the seeds of virtue should seek them from the Three Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse for the king and immediately rose from his seat to depart.

Regarding the *King Bimbisāra Visits the Buddha for Offerings Sūtra* (the right-hand sūtra): while the name of the sūtra and the translator are identical across all editions of the canon, its textual content is entirely the same in the Guo and Song editions, yet differs greatly from the Dan edition; it appears that the latter was not consulted in the process of selection.
Now, according to the *Kaiyuan lu*, it is stated:
"This sutra and the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the 'Chapter on Equal Vision' (*Samyag-dṛṣṭi-varga*), are translations of the same original text."
Upon examining the Guo and Song editions, they are identical to that [other] version; it is merely an excerpt from that sūtra. Why, then, is it considered a separate translation?

It seems that the Song Canon lost the translation by Dharmagupta, so this was copied from its original source as a separate circulation. However, since that *Ekottarika-āgama* was translated by Gautama Saṃghadeva of the Eastern Jin, why is it said to be the translation of Dharmagupta when it is an excerpt from that very sūtra?
Furthermore, as for all such transcribed scriptures that are not distinct translations, they were once deleted from the *Kaiyuan lu*; why then should this one alone remain?
Therefore, I now consider the edition in the Danzang (the Tibetan Canon) to be the authentic version.
